claims.text: Sliding contact in a corrosive environment produces an ultra-nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer in the HEA.
The tribo-induced surface layer governs a trade-off between improved wear behavior and degraded corrosion resistance.
Ultra-nanocrystalline HEAs can exhibit inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
The inverse Hall-Petch effect enhances the hardness of the refined surface layer.
The refined surface layer lowers friction.
The refined surface layer lowers the wear rate by increasing local hardness and altering shear behavior.
Residual stress and fine grains weaken the passive layer and reduce corrosion resistance in Cantor alloys.
Grain boundaries and defects in the refined layer provide diffusion pathways for aggressive chloride ions.
Sliding causes severe plastic deformation followed by rapid grain refinement or dynamic amorphization.
The initial HEA has a coarse-grained microstructure.
The initial HEA has an intact passive oxide film.
Tribo-corrosion produces a lower friction coefficient than a coarse-grained sample under static corrosion.
Tribo-corrosion produces a lower wear rate than the stated baseline.
Tribo-corrosion increases the corrosion rate by degrading the passive film.
Overall degradation is governed by an offset between improved wear characteristics and increased corrosion susceptibility.
The proposed response should occur in HEAs whose passive films are sensitive to microstructural defects.
The proposed response may fail in alloys with defect-tolerant or self-healing passive films.
The proposed response may fail when composition or processing history limits tribo-induced refinement.
The balance between wear reduction and corrosion acceleration depends on composition, sliding speed, load, and electrolyte concentration.

contradictions.description: The refined layer is said to gain hardness through the inverse Hall-Petch effect, but inverse Hall-Petch behavior denotes softening at very small grain sizes; the cited evidence explicitly describes it as softening.

The predicted friction and wear changes are framed relative to a static-corrosion baseline without sliding, for which friction coefficient and sliding wear rate are not defined, while the controlled comparison instead uses an inert sliding baseline.
